title: Distance Marching for Generative Modeling
claim: Following the distance field toward the data manifold keeps intermediate states closer to real samples, while the baseline drifts toward the data mean.
layout: Single wide panel, top-to-bottom descent through contour lines, ours vs baseline columns alternating
description: A single wide panel with wavy contour lines forming a distance field. The lines shade from red at the top (far from the data) to blue at the bottom (near the data). A dashed black curve with gray scatter points marks the data manifold at the bottom. The labels 'distance field', 'data mean' (with a star) and 'data manifold' sit along the center. Four columns each start with a noise image at the top. Two columns are labeled 'ours' (orange arrows) and two 'flow matching' (red arrows). Each column descends through intermediate images, shown with ellipsis dots, to a final image at the bottom: a dog in two columns and a weevil on a leaf in the other two. The 'ours' intermediates already show recognizable dog and weevil shapes. The flow matching intermediates are still noisy textures. The eye goes first to the noisy images and the colored contours, then down to the photos.
caption: We propose DISTANCE MARCHING to generate images without time input. Inspired by distance-field modeling, our method learns a denoising direction that focuses on closer targets. In contrast, the flow matching loss favors a direction biased toward the data mean in the early stages of generation. We compare outputs after 20% of the sampling steps to show that our sampling trajectories wander less. See Sec. 4 for a detailed analysis.
abstract: Modern generative models based on diffusion or flow matching transport noise toward the data manifold, without representing the data manifold explicitly. We propose Distance Marching that explores an alternative design by explicitly modeling a distance field of the data manifold. A distance field offers a geometric view of generation as a descent process toward the data manifold using only the current position. The negative gradient of the distance field provides the direction, and the distance value can optionally determine the step size. However, sparse training data in high-dimensional space make it difficult to identify the closest points on the data manifold needed to train the distance field. To address this challenge, we design new loss functions that emphasize denoising targets from closer data points. Our analysis shows that, without time input, emphasizing closer targets reduces denoising ambiguity and the bias toward the data mean. This distance-field perspective naturally motivates two principled deterministic samplers, showing fast convergence in inference. As a result, our model is the only one without time input that remains competitive with time-conditioned models across datasets and architectures. Moreover, our distance prediction is also helpful for early stopping during sampling and for out-of-distribution detection. We hope distance-field modeling can open a promising direction for exploring generative modeling from a geometric perspective.
